plan.contextChunk: This figure shows three U-tube manometer configurations that together cover every possible relationship between gas pressure and atmospheric pressure, each labeled with the corresponding pressure equation below. The left panel depicts a closed-end manometer whose sealed arm contains a vacuum, making the height difference h the sole determinant of pressure so that P_gas = hρg. The middle panel shows an open-end manometer in which the gas-side liquid stands higher than the open (atmospheric) side, indicating the gas is below atmospheric pressure and P_gas = P_atm − hρg. The right panel reverses that situation — the open-arm liquid is higher — indicating the gas exceeds atmospheric pressure so that P_gas = P_atm + hρg. This figure introduces the manometer as a practical pressure-measuring instrument and establishes the three distinct cases that determine which formula relates the liquid-column height h to the unknown gas pressure.

interactionPlan.concept: A U-tube manometer converts the difference between gas pressure and the pressure on the other arm (vacuum or atmosphere) into a measurable liquid height difference h, and which of three formulas applies depends on the manometer type and which side the liquid stands higher.
elements: three side-by-side U-tube manometer panels
lavender 'Gas' bulb with stopcock valve connecting to the left arm of each U-tube
gray liquid (mercury) filling the U-bend and rising to different heights in each arm
left panel: sealed right arm labeled 'Closed end' and 'Vacuum', liquid higher on the right arm
middle panel: open right arm labeled 'Open end' with downward arrow labeled 'P_atm', liquid higher on the gas (left) arm
right panel: open right arm labeled 'Open end' with 'P_atm' arrow, liquid higher on the open (right) arm
double-headed arrow labeled 'h' marking the height difference between the two liquid levels in each panel
horizontal reference lines at each liquid level
equation label under left panel: 'P_gas = hρg'
equation label under middle panel: 'P_gas = P_atm − hρg'
equation label under right panel: 'P_gas = P_atm + hρg'

interactions.label: Manometer configuration
interactions.teaches: The three configurations cover every possible relationship between P_gas and P_atm, and each one has its own formula — the instrument setup and the direction the liquid shifts determine which equation applies

interactions.label: Gas pressure P_gas (kPa)
interactions.teaches: Changing P_gas moves the liquid levels in real time: the height difference h grows or shrinks in direct proportion to how far the gas pressure is from the pressure on the other arm, and in the open-end case the liquid can swap which side is higher as P_gas crosses P_atm

Clicking the h arrow reveals the step-by-step derivation for the active configuration — pressure at equal liquid depths must be equal, so P_gas equals the reference pressure plus or minus the hρg column, with the sign set by which arm's liquid stands higher

demo_steps.title: Closed-end manometer
demo_steps.narration: With a vacuum sealed above the right arm, nothing pushes back on that side, so the entire height difference h is due to the gas alone: P_gas = hρg. This is an absolute pressure measurement.

demo_steps.title: Vary the gas pressure
demo_steps.narration: Drag the P_gas slider and watch both liquid levels respond — higher gas pressure pushes the gas-side liquid down and the vacuum-side liquid up, growing h proportionally.

demo_steps.title: Open end, gas below atmospheric
demo_steps.narration: Now the right arm is open to the atmosphere. Here the gas-side liquid stands higher, meaning the atmosphere pushes harder than the gas: P_gas = P_atm − hρg.

demo_steps.title: Open end, gas above atmospheric
demo_steps.narration: Raise P_gas above atmospheric pressure and the liquid shifts the other way — the open-arm liquid now stands higher, and the sign flips: P_gas = P_atm + hρg.

demo_steps.title: Why the formula works
demo_steps.narration: Click the h arrow: at the lower liquid surface, pressures from both sides must balance, so P_gas differs from the reference pressure by exactly the weight of the column hρg — the sign comes from which side's column is taller.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The height difference h measures how far the gas pressure is from the pressure on the other arm, and the plus-or-minus sign in the formula is read directly off which side of the U-tube the liquid stands higher.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Three panels shown one at a time per the toggle (the toggle is the comparison), each a gray-outlined U-tube with lavender gas bulb and stopcock on the left arm. Mercury rendered as gray shading with clear horizontal meniscus lines. Closed-end panel: sealed tube top with 'Closed end' / 'Vacuum' labels. Open-end panels: tube top open with a downward 'P_atm' arrow. Double-headed 'h' arrow beside the level difference, with thin horizontal reference lines from each meniscus. The active panel's equation (italic serif, e.g. P_gas = P_atm + hρg) appears below the tube and highlights when its configuration is selected. Liquid levels must animate smoothly and continuously as the P_gas slider moves, conserving total liquid (one side falls as the other rises); in open-end mode, crossing P_gas = P_atm levels the two columns (h = 0) before inverting. Clicking the h arrow opens a small derivation panel listing the pressure-balance steps for the active configuration.

authoredContext:
A manometer is a device similar to a barometer that can be used to measure the pressure of a gas trapped in a container. A closed-end manometer is a U-shaped tube with one closed arm, one arm that connects to the gas to be measured, and a nonvolatile liquid (usually mercury) in between. As with a barometer, the distance between the liquid levels in the two arms of the tube ( h in the diagram) is proportional to the pressure of the gas in the container. An open-end manometer ( ) is the same as a closed-end manometer, but one of its arms is open to the atmosphere. In this case, the distance between the liquid levels corresponds to the difference in pressure between the gas in the container and the atmosphere.

A manometer can be used to measure the pressure of a gas. The (difference in) height between the liquid levels ( h ) is a measure of the pressure. Mercury is usually used because of its large density.

Three diagrams of manometers are shown. Each manometer consists of a spherical pink container filled with gas on the left that is connected to a U-shaped, sealed tube by a valve on its right. The top of the U aligns with the gas-filled sphere and the U, which extends below, contains mercury. The first manometer has a sealed tube. The sealed end to the upper right in the diagram is labeled “closed end” and “vacuum.” The mercury level is higher in the right side of the tube than in the left. The difference in height is labeled “h.” Beneath this manometer illustration appears the label P subscript gas equal sign h rho g. The second manometer has an open-ended tube, which is labeled “open end.” At this opening in the upper right of the diagram is the label P subscript atm. The mercury level is higher in the left side of the tube than in the right. This difference in height is labeled “h.” Beneath this manometer illustration appears the label P subscript gas equal sign P subscript atm minus sign h rho g. The third manometer has an open-ended tube and is similar to the second manometer except that the mercury level is higher in the right side of the tube than in the left. This difference in height is labeled “h.” Beneath this manometer illustration appears the label P subscript gas equal sign P subscript a t m plus h rho g.

discrepancies: In the default rendered state the bottom equation appears to read '= hρg' — the leading 'P_gas' (P with 'gas' subscript) is missing or clipped, likely because eqText.text() is called and then eqText.clear() before tspans are appended and re-centered

The source shows the three manometer cases side-by-side for direct comparison; the generated figure shows only one at a time behind radio buttons/steps, so the sign contrast between the −hρg and +hρg cases is never visible simultaneously
The closed end of the tube is a flat black cap line rather than the sealed rounded tube end shown in the source, and the stopcock/valve is a crossed box rather than the recognizable valve symbol
The gas bulb connects directly to the tube top with no bent hose/neck as in the source, and the bulb is smaller relative to the tube than in the original
evaluation.notes: The U-tube, meniscus levels, h arrow, and per-case equations are physically correct and the mode toggle/slider/step player/derivation popup are rich, well-wired interactions; the main flaws are the apparently truncated default equation label and the loss of the source's side-by-side three-case comparison (partially justified by the toggle pattern).
action_items: Fix the equation rendering: remove the redundant eqText.text(eq...) call before eqText.clear() and verify the 'P' + 'gas' subscript tspan actually displays in the default closed-end state (screenshot shows only '= hρg')
Give the closed-end arm a sealed rounded cap (or clearly closed tip) instead of a flat horizontal stroke to match the source's sealed tube
Replace the crossed-box stopcock with a small valve symbol closer to the original hardware drawing
Consider a 'compare all three' view or thumbnail strip so students can see the −/+/absolute cases simultaneously as in the source layout

discrepancies: the source presents all three manometer cases side-by-side as the primary composition; the generated figure defaults to only the closed-end case, with the other two behind radio buttons or a scaled-down 'Compare all three' mode

in the source's closed-end panel the h arrow is drawn inside the right arm between the two levels; the generated figure draws it as a separate dimension line with extension lines to the right of the tube (acceptable, but a different drafting style)
the mercury/fluid in the source is drawn as a filled shaded column with visible surface shading; the generated figure renders it as a flat gray stroke, losing the liquid-column look
the 'Compare all three' panels are scaled to 0.42, making their labels and equations quite small compared to the source's full-size three-panel layout
evaluation.notes: A faithful and pedagogically strong manometer figure: correct U-tube geometry, gas bulb, stopcock, vacuum/open-end variants, h dimensioning, and the three correct formulas, plus a working pressure slider, mode radios, demo steps, and a derivation popup; main losses are the three-panel composition being hidden behind toggles and the flat-stroke rendering of the liquid column.
action_items: Consider making the three-panel side-by-side comparison the default view (or a more prominent option) to match the source's composition at a glance.
Render the liquid as a filled region with a slight vertical gradient or shading instead of a uniform gray stroke so it reads as a liquid column.
Increase the scale or available width of the 'Compare all three' sub-panels so their equations and labels remain comfortably legible.

feedback.rationale: No failure modes, strong scores across all dimensions (average 4.4, concept and interactivity at 5), and the remaining discrepancies are minor stylistic polish (default view choice, liquid shading, sub-panel scale) that don't undermine the figure's faithfulness or pedagogical value.
